### ⏱️ No Notes, No Peeking

**Three questions. Sixty seconds each. Write your answer before I reveal it.**

Reading the answer twice teaches you nothing. Getting it wrong once and correcting it does.

---

### ⚡ Q1 — What Is Line 4?

<pre class="fastq-record"><code>@SRR8836894.1 1/1
GTCGGAGCACATCTTGCTGGCCCAGGTGTTCAGCAAGATGGAGCAGGTGTCTGGCGTG
+
+AFA<strong class="q40">I</strong>&lt;FFF77&lt;AF-AAF7FAAJJJ7JFAJ-FFF-FF--7---F&lt;&lt;F&lt;AJJFFAFJJAJ-</code></pre>

**Line 4 is a quality string.** In it, the character **`I`** appears.

1. What does `I` mean?
2. What is the probability that base is wrong?

**ASCII table (excerpt)** — use it to decode `I`:

| ASCII | 70 | 71 | 72 | 73 | 74 |
|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| Char | `F` | `G` | `H` | **`I`** | `J` |

<div class="small muted">Phred+33: <strong>Phred = ASCII − 33</strong>.</div>

---

### ✅ A1 — Quality, Position by Position

1. **What does `I` mean?** From the table, `I` is ASCII 73. Phred+33: **73 − 33 = Q40**.
2. **What is the probability that base is wrong?** 10<sup>−4</sup> — **one wrong base in 10,000**.

$$P(\text{error}) = 10^{-Q/10} = 10^{-4}$$

- Q30 = 1 in 1,000. Q20 = 1 in 100.
- The quality string is **positionally locked** to the sequence: base 57 and quality 57 describe the same nucleotide.

::: {.callout-note}
A trimmer edits **line 2 and line 4 together**. Editing only one corrupts the record.
:::

---

### ⚡ Q2 — Do You Trim?

![](https://www.bioinformatics.babraham.ac.uk/projects/fastqc/fastqc.png){fig-align="center" width="65%"}

<div class="credit">FastQC project, Babraham Institute (Andrew Andrews)</div>

**Does this require trimming? If yes, exactly what — and what do you leave alone?**

---

### ✅ A2 — Trim What the Plot Shows

**Trim adapters and the low-quality tail. Do not trim the whole read.**

- Adapter read-through means the insert was shorter than 150 bp.
- The last ~30 bp carry most of the errors.
- A typical setting: Q20–Q25 tail trim, minimum length 30–36.

**In this lecture, the trimming is already done — we inherit the cleaned files.**

::: {.callout-important}
Trimming is not a ritual. **The plot is the evidence.** A clean library does not need aggressive trimming — and over-trimming creates “too short” reads that never align.
:::

---

### ⚡ Q3 — Can STAR Run?

After trimming:

- `R1` has **4,998,000** records.
- `R2` has **5,000,000** records.

**Can you align these two files together?**

---

### ✅ A3 — Mates Must Stay in Lockstep

**No.** STAR reads mate 1 and mate 2 together, record by record. Unequal counts mean the pairing is broken.

First check:

```bash
wc -l R1.fastq R2.fastq    # both must be equal, and divisible by 4
```

Usual cause: the trimmer ran in single-end mode, or one mate was filtered out.

::: {.callout-note}
Before alignment, prove the two files still describe the **same fragments**. This is a 5-second check that saves an hour.
:::

## 🧩 2. The Alignment Problem

::: {.agenda data-section="2"}
:::

---

### We have our reads ready… Now what?

A read is a 150-letter fragment. The genome is 3 billion letters.

- **RefSeq (3 Gbp):** <code><strong>ACGTA</strong>GCTTAGTTGC<strong>ACGTA</strong></code>
- **A read (150 bp):** <code><strong>ACGTA</strong></code>

**Where does this read belong?**

---


### What “Align” Means
**Alignment = the position and strand where that fragment best matches the reference.**

![](https://training.galaxyproject.org/training-material/topics/sequence-analysis/images/mapping/mapping.png){fig-align="center" width="70%"}

<div class="credit">Galaxy Training Network, “Mapping” tutorial (J. Wolff, B. Batut, H. Koch), CC BY 4.0</div>

::: {.callout-note}
“Where does it map?” is not one question. It is **where, how well, and how sure**.
:::

---

### Why Exact Matching Fails? — Errors & Variants

![](../_assets/exact_match_variants.png){fig-align="center" width="88%"}

- **Sequencing errors:** ~0.1–1% of bases are wrong.
- **Variants:** a SNP or indel can still be the correct read.

::: {.callout-important}
One mismatch breaks an exact match — even when the read is biologically correct.
:::

---

### Why Exact Matching Fails? — Repeats

![](../_assets/repeat_multi_mapping.png){fig-align="center" width="85%"}

Millions of bases occur in many places. One read can have dozens of equally good homes.

::: {.callout-note}
Exact matching returns many hits; the aligner must choose.
:::

---

### Why Exact Matching Fails? — Strandedness

![](../_assets/strandedness.png){fig-align="center" width="85%"}

Every read has a reverse complement. The search must consider both orientations.

::: {.callout-note}
A perfect match on the reverse strand is still a perfect match.
:::

---

### RNASeq data is astronomically HUGE!

**150 bp** against **3 Gbp**.

::: {.callout-important}
Naive search: 3 Gbp × 50 M reads. **Impossible.** The index makes it possible.
:::

---

### The RNA-seq Twist: Splicing

![](../_assets/splicing_before_after.png){fig-align="center" width="88%"}

<div class="quote">
The read is contiguous. The genome is not.
</div>

An RNA-seq read can span an exon–exon junction. The aligner must **split the read** and invent an intron — not reject it as a bad match.

---

### Two Ways to Align

| | Genome aligner | Pseudo-aligner |
|---|---|---|
| Examples | STAR, HISAT2 | salmon, kallisto |
| Output | **BAM** with coordinates | counts, no BAM |
| Splicing | explicit junctions | k-mer compatibility |
| Use here | QC, IGV, counting, Space Ranger | fast expression estimates |

::: {.callout-note}
We need a **BAM**: it is the object we QC, the object we count, and the object Space Ranger produces. That is why we use STAR.
:::

---

### Key Notes — The Alignment Problem

- **A read is contiguous. The genome is not.** A 100 bp read can be 40 bp exon 1 + 60 bp exon 2.
- **Exact matching fails** on sequencing errors, repeats, strand, and splicing.
- **Split alignment:** `40M + intron + 60M`. The aligner searches for the gap — it does not reject the read.
- **We need a BAM**, so we choose **STAR**.

---

### We know the problem. Now the machine.

The aligner must find a short, imperfect, possibly split match in 3 billion letters.

::: {.callout-note}
Next: how STAR solves it — the suffix index, the maximal mappable prefix, and the stitch across introns.
:::

---

## ⚙️ 3. STAR 101

::: {.agenda data-section="3"}
:::

---

### STAR — Spliced Transcripts Alignment to a Reference

<div class="quote">
STAR indexes every suffix of the genome, finds the longest exact prefix of each read, extends it, and stitches the pieces across introns.
</div>

::: {.callout-note}
Dobin et al., *Bioinformatics* 2013. “Ultrafast” is not magic — it is an uncompressed index held in RAM.
:::

---

### What STAR Does

**Four moves — for every read:**

1. **Index** — build the search structure once.
2. **Seed** — find the maximal mappable prefix (MMP).
3. **Extend** — add mismatches and gaps, scoring each extension.
4. **Stitch** — re-seed downstream when an exon boundary interrupts.

---

### What STAR Needs

| Input | What it is | Why STAR needs it |
|---|---|---|
| FASTA | the genome sequence | the text being searched |
| GTF | exons, transcripts, genes | known splice junctions + gene models |
| **Index** | a precomputed search structure | the difference between hours and seconds |

Next: how STAR builds and uses the index.

---

### 🖥️ Colab Session — Start the Index

::: {.part}
<div class="label">Start the index now</div>

- Run the `genomeGenerate` cell **in the background**.
- Then `tail -f data/star_index/Log.out` once, to prove it is alive.
- **Do not wait.** It takes ~25 min on 2 vCPUs; we will spend exactly that long on the next slides.
:::

```bash
STAR --runMode genomeGenerate \
     --genomeDir data/star_index \
     --genomeFastaFiles data/ref/Homo_sapiens.GRCh38.dna.primary_assembly.sub.fa \
     --sjdbGTFfile data/gtf/Homo_sapiens.GRCh38.sub.gtf \
     --sjdbOverhang 149 --genomeSAindexNbases 12 \
     --genomeSAsparseD 1 --runThreadN 2
# full nohup ... & command is in the notebook
```

---

### Index — Every Position, Sorted

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="62%"}
![](../_assets/suffix_tails.png){fig-align="center" width="100%"}
:::

::: {.column width="38%"}
- **One row per position**: the letters from that position to the end.

Ours: 181 Mb → **180 million rows**, built once by `genomeGenerate`.
:::

::::

---

### Index — Sorted by Letters

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="62%"}
![](../_assets/suffix_sorted.png){fig-align="center" width="100%"}
:::

::: {.column width="38%"}
- **Sorted by letters**, the **start** column jumps around. That list is the index.
- The first letter picks the block, the next letter narrows it.
:::

::::

---

### Index — Lookup, Not Scan

Read `GTACGT` against the sorted list: one pass, narrowed at every letter.

![](../_assets/suffix_lookup.png){fig-align="center" width="100%"}

That is why STAR aligns 5,000 read pairs in **23 s**, not hours.

---

### Index — The Cost: RAM

The list is held in RAM, whole, for the entire run.

| reference | index on disk |
|---|---|
| 181 Mb (chr17/21/22) | **1.7 GB** |
| whole genome (3.1 Gb) | ~28 GB |

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}
- The letters are cheap: **189 MB**.
- The **positions** are the heavy part: **1.4 GB**.
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
`--genomeSAsparseD` trades memory for lookup speed:

- `1` — store every position: measured **1.4 GB** (our run)
- `2` — store every second: measured **638 MB**, slower lookup
:::

::::

---

### Seed — The Longest Exact Match

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="44%"}
![](../_assets/star_step1.png){fig-align="center" width="100%"}

<div class="credit">HBC Intro-to-RNA-seq, CC BY 4.0 — adapted from STAR Fig. 1</div>
:::

::: {.column width="56%"}
STAR takes the read and finds the longest sequence that matches the reference **exactly** — the **maximal mappable prefix (MMP)**, called **seed1**.

Everything past seed1 is left unmapped, for now.
:::

::::

---

### Seed — Searching Only the Unmapped Part

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="44%"}
![](../_assets/star_step2.png){fig-align="center" width="100%"}

<div class="credit">HBC Intro-to-RNA-seq, CC BY 4.0 — adapted from STAR Fig. 1</div>
:::

::: {.column width="56%"}
STAR then searches **only the unmapped part** of the read and finds its MMP: **seed2**.

seed2 lands far downstream, between a **donor** and an **acceptor** site — the two ends of an intron. The gap between seed1 and seed2 is the intron this read spliced over.

Searching one unmapped piece at a time is what makes STAR fast.
:::

::::

---

### Seed — Unique, Not Long

A seed does not have to be long to be useful. It only has to be **unique enough** to anchor the search.

A seed that appears everywhere anchors nothing: STAR only uses seeds that map to fewer than **10,000** places in the genome (`--seedMultimapNmax 10000`, STAR's default, which we left alone).

---

### Extend — When Nothing Matches Exactly

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="44%"}
![](../_assets/star_step3.png){fig-align="center" width="85%"}

<div class="credit">HBC Intro-to-RNA-seq, CC BY 4.0 — adapted from STAR Fig. 1</div>
:::

::: {.column width="56%"}
If the rest of the read has no exact match — a mismatch, an indel, a low-quality base — the previous seeds are **extended**, base by base, scoring every base added.

The red bar is a mismatch accepted during extension.
:::

::::

---

### Extend — The Soft Clip

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="44%"}
![](../_assets/star_step4.png){fig-align="center" width="100%"}

<div class="credit">HBC Intro-to-RNA-seq, CC BY 4.0 — adapted from STAR Fig. 1</div>
:::

::: {.column width="56%"}
When extension does not give a good alignment, the end of the read is **soft clipped**: adapter, poor quality, or contaminating sequence.

The clipped bases are not thrown away: they stay in the record, marked `S` in the CIGAR, outside the aligned blocks.
:::

::::

---

### Stitch — Clustering and Scoring

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="44%"}
![](../_assets/star_step5.png){fig-align="center" width="100%"}

<div class="credit">HBC Intro-to-RNA-seq, CC BY 4.0 — adapted from STAR Fig. 1</div>
:::

::: {.column width="56%"}
Seeds are clustered around **anchor seeds** — seeds that map to one place only — then stitched into one alignment, scored by mismatches, indels, and gaps.

The dashed line in the stitched read is the intron.

::: {.callout-important}
Stitching is what makes STAR **splice-aware**. 

A DNA aligner would stop at the exon boundary; STAR starts a second search.
:::
:::

::::

---

### Stitch — Crossing an Exon Boundary

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="70%"}

![A real spliced record: 110M, a 7,018 bp intron, 40M](../_assets/stitch_cigar.png){fig-align="center" width="100%"}

:::

::: {.column width="30%"}

| piece | meaning |
|---|---|
| `110M` | 110 bp aligned to exon 1 |
| `7018N` | 7,018 bp skipped — an intron |
| `40M` | 40 bp aligned to exon 2 |

- the read never loses bases; the **genome**
  skips them

- `N` is RNA-seq's signature

:::

::::

---

### Stitch — Annotated vs Novel Junctions

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="70%"}

![An annotated junction, flanked by 149 bp; a novel junction needing 8 bp](../_assets/stitch_junctions.png){fig-align="center" width="100%"}

:::

::: {.column width="30%"}

| | annotated | novel |
|---|---|---|
| source | GTF, baked into the index | found by the reads |
| cost | cheap, already known | must earn its place |
| control | `--sjdbGTFfile` | `--alignSJoverhangMin 8` |
| trust | high | lower, needs support |

:::

::::

::: {.small .muted}
Known junctions are the difference between a fast alignment and a search
through every possible intron. `--sjdbOverhang` = read length − 1 = 149.
:::

---

### The Flags, Mapped to the Algorithm

![](../_assets/flags_map.png){fig-align="center" width="100%"}

---

### The Flags We Set

| flag | value | what it controls |
|---|---|---|
| `--genomeSAindexNbases` | 12 | lookup prefix; default 14 segfaults |
| `--genomeSAsparseD` | 1 | dense suffix array: more RAM, faster |
| `--sjdbGTFfile` | GTF | known junctions in the index |
| `--sjdbOverhang` | 149 | exon sequence flanking each junction |
| `--outFilterMultimapNmax` | 20 | maximum loci reported per read |
| `--outFilterType` | `BySJout` | junction-consistency filter |
| `--outSAMtype` | `BAM SortedByCoordinate` | sorted output, ready to index |
| `--alignSJoverhangMin` | 8 | minimum overhang at a novel junction (default 5) |
| `--alignSJDBoverhangMin` | 1 | minimum overhang at an annotated junction (default 3) |

::: {.small .muted}
`BySJout` is a junction-consistency filter, **not** a uniqueness filter. A read
can be unique and still be filtered if its junction is implausible.
:::

---

### 🎯 Flags Are Two Decisions

<div class="quote">
The index decides what the aligner can find. The run decides what the file reports.
</div>

- **At index build** — prefix 12, sparse 1, junctions from the GTF, 149 bp of
  flanking exon: four choices about what is visible at all.
- **At the run** — 20 loci per read, `BySJout`, overhang minimums 8 and 1,
  sorted BAM: four choices about what survives into the file.

::: {.callout-important}
The flags you did **not** set are decisions too. `--seedMultimapNmax 10000` is
STAR’s default, so every stitch step that maps fewer than 10,000 places is
allowed. `--runThreadN 16` is not a default: it is your machine.
:::

---

## 🧾 4. Reading a BAM

::: {.agenda data-section="4"}
:::

---

### SAM, BAM, CRAM

| Format | What it is | When you meet it |
|---|---|---|
| **SAM** | plain text, one line per alignment | debugging, `samtools view` |
| **BAM** | binary, compressed, indexable | the working format |
| **CRAM** | reference-compressed | long-term archives |

::: {.callout-note}
BAM is the **interchange format**: IGV reads it, featureCounts reads it, GATK reads it, Space Ranger writes it. Learn one, and the rest of the course can read the file.
:::

---

### The Header Is the Provenance

```text
@HD  VN:1.6  SO:coordinate
@SQ  SN:17  LN:83257441
@SQ  SN:21  LN:46709983
@SQ  SN:22  LN:50818468
@PG  ID:STAR  PN:STAR  VN:2.7.11b
     CL:STAR --runMode alignReads --genomeDir data/star_index ...
```

- `@HD` — file format and sort order.
- `@SQ` — the reference dictionary: names and lengths.
- `@PG` — the **exact command** that made the file.

::: {.callout-important}
The BAM remembers how it was made. That is reproducibility you do not have to reconstruct from memory.
:::

---

### QNAME and FLAG

<table class="rec">
<tr><th class="key">QNAME</th><th class="key">FLAG</th><th class="fade">RNAME</th><th class="fade">POS</th><th class="fade">MAPQ</th><th class="fade">CIGAR</th><th class="fade">RNEXT</th><th class="fade">PNEXT</th><th class="fade">TLEN</th><th class="fade">SEQ</th><th class="fade">QUAL</th><th class="fade">tags</th></tr>
<tr><td class="key">SRR8836894.3781</td><td class="key">99</td><td class="fade">17</td><td class="fade">79100</td><td class="fade">255</td><td class="fade">110M7018N40M</td><td class="fade">=</td><td class="fade">79158</td><td class="fade">7225</td><td class="fade">GGCACAATGGCT…</td><td class="fade">AAFFFJJFAAJ&lt;…</td><td class="fade">NH:i:1 AS:i:282 …</td></tr>
</table>

- `QNAME` is the read's name. Mates share it: `SRR8836894.3781` appears
  twice in our BAM, once per end of the pair.
- `FLAG` is a **sum of bits**: 99 = 1 + 2 + 32 + 64. Paired, proper pair,
  mate on the forward strand, this record is read 1.
- 300 records at 99, 300 at 147, out of 1,472. `FLAG` gets its own slide.

---

### FLAG, Decoded

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="70%"}

![Four flags from our BAM, decomposed into the bits that sum to them](../_assets/bam_flag.png){fig-align="center" width="100%"}

:::

::: {.column width="30%"}

- the bits **sum** to the number: 99 = 1 + 2 + 32 + 64

- 4, 8: *unmapped, no mate* — special cases;
  512, 1024: secondary, duplicate

- 2, 4, 8, 512, 1024 are mutually exclusive;
  1, 16, 32, 64, 128 combine freely

:::

::::

::: {.small .muted}
99 and 147 are the normal pair, and they are exactly half of our BAM:
300 + 300. If you remember two numbers, remember those.
:::

---

### RNAME and POS

<table class="rec">
<tr><th class="fade">QNAME</th><th class="fade">FLAG</th><th class="key">RNAME</th><th class="key">POS</th><th class="fade">MAPQ</th><th class="fade">CIGAR</th><th class="fade">RNEXT</th><th class="fade">PNEXT</th><th class="fade">TLEN</th><th class="fade">SEQ</th><th class="fade">QUAL</th><th class="fade">tags</th></tr>
<tr><td class="fade">SRR8836894.3781</td><td class="fade">99</td><td class="key">17</td><td class="key">79100</td><td class="fade">255</td><td class="fade">110M7018N40M</td><td class="fade">=</td><td class="fade">79158</td><td class="fade">7225</td><td class="fade">GGCACAATGGCT…</td><td class="fade">AAFFFJJFAAJ&lt;…</td><td class="fade">NH:i:1 AS:i:282 …</td></tr>
</table>

- `RNAME` is the contig as STAR wrote it: `17`, not `chr17`.
- `POS` is 1-based, the leftmost **aligned** base: `79100`.
- With a spliced CIGAR, `POS` is the left end of the *first* block. This
  record ends at `86267`; `POS` + read length is not the end.

---

### MAPQ

<table class="rec">
<tr><th class="fade">QNAME</th><th class="fade">FLAG</th><th class="fade">RNAME</th><th class="fade">POS</th><th class="key">MAPQ</th><th class="fade">CIGAR</th><th class="fade">RNEXT</th><th class="fade">PNEXT</th><th class="fade">TLEN</th><th class="fade">SEQ</th><th class="fade">QUAL</th><th class="fade">tags</th></tr>
<tr><td class="fade">SRR8836894.3781</td><td class="fade">99</td><td class="fade">17</td><td class="fade">79100</td><td class="key">255</td><td class="fade">110M7018N40M</td><td class="fade">=</td><td class="fade">79158</td><td class="fade">7225</td><td class="fade">GGCACAATGGCT…</td><td class="fade">AAFFFJJFAAJ&lt;…</td><td class="fade">NH:i:1 AS:i:282 …</td></tr>
</table>

- `MAPQ` answers: *how much do you trust this placement?*
- 255 means one place in the genome. 1,106 of our 1,230 primary records
  are 255.
- 48 records are `MAPQ 3`, 76 are `MAPQ 1` — they fit in more than one
  place, and STAR is telling you.
- A low `MAPQ` is not a bad read. It is an honest read.

::: {.small .muted}
`MAPQ` gets the next slide, with the distribution.
:::

---

### MAPQ Distribution

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="65%"}

![MAPQ distribution in our BAM: 1,106 primary records at 255, 124 below](../_assets/bam_mapq.png){fig-align="center" width="100%"}

:::

::: {.column width="35%"}

| `MAPQ` | measured in our BAM |
|---|---|
| **255** | **one place** — 1,106 primary records |
| 124 records below | shown in the figure |

- 124 primary records are lower than 255: 48 at `MAPQ 3`, 76 at `MAPQ 1`

- `Log.final.out` counts them: 553 uniquely mapped (11.06%), 62 mapped
  to multiple loci (1.24%)

:::

::::

::: {.small .muted}
Low `MAPQ` is honesty, not failure: the read fits in more than one place,
and STAR is telling you so. The `NH` tag, at the end of the record, is
where STAR writes that number down.
:::

---

### CIGAR

<table class="rec">
<tr><th class="fade">QNAME</th><th class="fade">FLAG</th><th class="fade">RNAME</th><th class="fade">POS</th><th class="fade">MAPQ</th><th class="key">CIGAR</th><th class="fade">RNEXT</th><th class="fade">PNEXT</th><th class="fade">TLEN</th><th class="fade">SEQ</th><th class="fade">QUAL</th><th class="fade">tags</th></tr>
<tr><td class="fade">SRR8836894.3781</td><td class="fade">99</td><td class="fade">17</td><td class="fade">79100</td><td class="fade">255</td><td class="key">110M7018N40M</td><td class="fade">=</td><td class="fade">79158</td><td class="fade">7225</td><td class="fade">GGCACAATGGCT…</td><td class="fade">AAFFFJJFAAJ&lt;…</td><td class="fade">NH:i:1 AS:i:282 …</td></tr>
</table>

- `110M7018N40M`: 110 aligned, 7,018 skipped, 40 aligned.
- `N` is the intron. The genome jumps; the read loses nothing.
- Reference span `79100–86267`, measured from the record. `CIGAR` gets its
  own slide, with the figure.

---

### CIGAR, Decoded

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="70%"}

![A spliced record: 110M, then a 7,018 bp gap, then 40M](../_assets/bam_cigar.png){fig-align="center" width="100%"}

:::

::: {.column width="30%"}

- `M` aligned · `I` insert in read · `D` delete from
  reference · `N` intron · `S` soft-clip

- `5M10I` = five aligned, ten inserted: **an insertion**

- `S` bases are in the `SEQ` but not counted in `POS`

:::

::::

::: {.callout-important}
`N` is not a deletion. The read did not lose 7,018 bases — the **genome**
skips them. That is a spliced alignment.
:::

**You will see this arc in IGV, Section 5.**

---

### RNEXT and PNEXT

<table class="rec">
<tr><th class="fade">QNAME</th><th class="fade">FLAG</th><th class="fade">RNAME</th><th class="fade">POS</th><th class="fade">MAPQ</th><th class="fade">CIGAR</th><th class="key">RNEXT</th><th class="key">PNEXT</th><th class="fade">TLEN</th><th class="fade">SEQ</th><th class="fade">QUAL</th><th class="fade">tags</th></tr>
<tr><td class="fade">SRR8836894.3781</td><td class="fade">99</td><td class="fade">17</td><td class="fade">79100</td><td class="fade">255</td><td class="fade">110M7018N40M</td><td class="key">=</td><td class="key">79158</td><td class="fade">7225</td><td class="fade">GGCACAATGGCT…</td><td class="fade">AAFFFJJFAAJ&lt;…</td><td class="fade">NH:i:1 AS:i:282 …</td></tr>
</table>

- `RNEXT` is the mate's contig. `=` means *the same chromosome as this
  record*.
- `PNEXT` is the mate's `POS`: `79158`, 58 bases to the right.
- The mate is flag `147`, `52M7018N97M1S`, ending `86324`. Same read name,
  same intron, opposite end of the fragment.

---

### TLEN

<table class="rec">
<tr><th class="fade">QNAME</th><th class="fade">FLAG</th><th class="fade">RNAME</th><th class="fade">POS</th><th class="fade">MAPQ</th><th class="fade">CIGAR</th><th class="fade">RNEXT</th><th class="fade">PNEXT</th><th class="key">TLEN</th><th class="fade">SEQ</th><th class="fade">QUAL</th><th class="fade">tags</th></tr>
<tr><td class="fade">SRR8836894.3781</td><td class="fade">99</td><td class="fade">17</td><td class="fade">79100</td><td class="fade">255</td><td class="fade">110M7018N40M</td><td class="fade">=</td><td class="fade">79158</td><td class="key">7225</td><td class="fade">GGCACAATGGCT…</td><td class="fade">AAFFFJJFAAJ&lt;…</td><td class="fade">NH:i:1 AS:i:282 …</td></tr>
</table>

- `TLEN 7225` is the **fragment**: leftmost start `79100` to rightmost
  end `86324`, counted across the intron.
- The sign is read–mate order: `+7225` on flag 99, `-7225` on flag 147.
- Not the gap between the two `POS` — `79158 - 79100` is 58. `TLEN` is
  what library prep calls fragment size.

---

### SEQ and QUAL

<table class="rec">
<tr><th class="fade">QNAME</th><th class="fade">FLAG</th><th class="fade">RNAME</th><th class="fade">POS</th><th class="fade">MAPQ</th><th class="fade">CIGAR</th><th class="fade">RNEXT</th><th class="fade">PNEXT</th><th class="fade">TLEN</th><th class="key">SEQ</th><th class="key">QUAL</th><th class="fade">tags</th></tr>
<tr><td class="fade">SRR8836894.3781</td><td class="fade">99</td><td class="fade">17</td><td class="fade">79100</td><td class="fade">255</td><td class="fade">110M7018N40M</td><td class="fade">=</td><td class="fade">79158</td><td class="fade">7225</td><td class="key">GGCACAATGGCT…</td><td class="key">AAFFFJJFAAJ&lt;…</td><td class="fade">NH:i:1 AS:i:282 …</td></tr>
</table>

- `SEQ` is the read, 150 bases. It includes bases the aligner did not
  match: the mate's `52M7018N97M1S` aligns 149 and **soft-clips 1**.

::: {.small .muted}
- `QUAL` is one character per base, same length as `SEQ`:
  `# ) - 7 < A F J` in our BAM.
- Phred: character − 33, so `#` is Q2, `J` is Q41.
:::

---

### The STAR Tags

<table class="rec">
<tr><th class="fade">QNAME</th><th class="fade">FLAG</th><th class="fade">RNAME</th><th class="fade">POS</th><th class="fade">MAPQ</th><th class="fade">CIGAR</th><th class="fade">RNEXT</th><th class="fade">PNEXT</th><th class="fade">TLEN</th><th class="fade">SEQ</th><th class="fade">QUAL</th><th class="key">tags</th></tr>
<tr><td class="fade">SRR8836894.3781</td><td class="fade">99</td><td class="fade">17</td><td class="fade">79100</td><td class="fade">255</td><td class="fade">110M7018N40M</td><td class="fade">=</td><td class="fade">79158</td><td class="fade">7225</td><td class="fade">GGCACAATGGCT…</td><td class="fade">AAFFFJJFAAJ&lt;…</td><td class="key">NH:i:1 AS:i:282 …</td></tr>
</table>

- `NH:i:1` — the number of loci STAR found. This is why `MAPQ` drops:
  `NH:i:2` records carry `MAPQ 3`, `NH:i:3` and `NH:i:4` carry `MAPQ 1`.
- `AS:i:282` — STAR's alignment score for this record.
- `HI:i:1` — hard-clip count STAR records for the read.
- `nM:i:7` — STAR's own mismatch-related count. Comparing aligned bases
  to `chr17.fa` gives 4 mismatches, so `nM` is not just "mismatches";
  read it as STAR's count, not a base-by-base tally.

::: {.small .muted}
Tags come after the 11 mandatory fields, on the same line.
`samtools view` prints them.
:::

---

### Reading the Columns

| what you ask | column | example |
|---|---|---|
| which read? | `QNAME` | `SRR8836894.3781` |
| pair? mate? mapped? | `FLAG` | `99` |
| **where?** | `RNAME`, `POS` | `17`, `79100` |
| **how sure?** | `MAPQ` | `255` |
| **what shape?** | `CIGAR` | `110M7018N40M` |
| bases, quality | `SEQ`, `QUAL` | 150 letters, Phred |
| mate position | `RNEXT`, `PNEXT` | `=`, `79158` |
| fragment length | `TLEN` | `7225` |

---

### Sort, Index, `.bai`

1. **Coordinate sort** — records ordered by chromosome and position.
2. **Index** — a lookup table from region to file offset.
3. **Random access** — IGV and `samtools view file region` become instant.

```bash
samtools index sample.Aligned.sortedByCoord.out.bam
```

::: {.callout-important}
`samtools idxstats` and region queries need the `.bai`. Without it, they fail with “random alignment retrieval only works for indexed BAMs.” Build the index; do not work around it.
:::

---

### What STAR Writes

| File | What it is | Use today |
|---|---|---|
| `*.Aligned.sortedByCoord.out.bam` | sorted alignments | yes |
| `*.Log.final.out` | summary metrics | **yes** |
| `*.Log.out` | every parameter and step | debugging |
| `*.Log.progress.out` | live progress | while it runs |
| `*.SJ.out.tab` | splice junctions | **yes** |
| `_STARtmp/` | temporary sort files | delete after success |

::: {.callout-note}
Three files carry the lecture: the **BAM** (evidence), `Log.final.out` (the aligner’s opinion), and `SJ.out.tab` (where the introns are).
:::

---

### 🧰 Also in a Real Pipeline

| Flag | What it buys you |
|---|---|
| `--readFilesCommand zcat` | align `.fastq.gz` directly — no manual decompression |
| `--outReadsUnmapped Fastx` | write the unmapped reads, so you can BLAST them and find contamination |
| `--quantMode GeneCounts` | STAR counts per gene itself — an alternative to featureCounts |
| `--outSAMattrRGline` | read groups, needed downstream by GATK (not by counting) |

::: {.callout-note}
None of these change the concepts. They are the difference between a notebook and a production pipeline.
:::

### ✍️ Decode This Record

<div class="record"><span class="hl2">SRR8836894.3116</span>  <span class="hl">99</span>  17  1875710  <span class="hl">255</span>  <span class="hl">84M1418N66M</span>  =  1878996  3589  <span class="hl">NH:i:1</span></div>

1. Is this read paired?
2. Is the pair proper?
3. Which mate is it?
4. How many loci does it have?
5. Is it spliced — and how do you know?

---

### ✅ Decode This Record — Answers

1. **Paired** — bit 1 is set.
2. **Proper pair** — bit 2 is set.
3. **First in pair** — bit 64; mate is reverse (bit 32).
4. **One locus** — MAPQ 255; `NH:i:1`.
5. **Spliced** — `1418N` in the CIGAR: 84 bp exon, 1,418 bp intron, 66 bp exon, and 84 + 66 = 150 bp of read.

::: {.callout-tip}
`TLEN 3589` spans from this read’s start (1,875,710) to its mate’s end (1,879,298). It is the insert size — which the next section will use as a QC check.
:::

---

### 🎯 One Line, Five Claims

<div class="quote">
The record states where, how, and how well. Every claim can be re-derived from the columns.
</div>

- `17  1875710` is the **address**: chromosome, then 1-based start.
- `99` is the **shape**: paired, proper, first of the pair, mate on the reverse.
- `84M1418N66M` is the **geometry**: exon, intron, exon.
- `255` with `NH:i:1` is the **confidence**: one locus, STAR’s top score.
- `3589` is the **pair**: this read’s start to its mate’s end.

::: {.callout-important}
This record is `SRR8836894.3116` from our own STAR run, not an invented example. Its mate reads `147  17  1878996  255  66M153N84M`, the same pair seen from the other side.
:::

## 📊 5. QC: Trust, but Verify

::: {.agenda data-section="5"}
:::

---

### Two Layers of QC

<div class="grid2">
<div class="card">
<h4>The aligner’s opinion</h4>
<p><code>Log.final.out</code> — how many reads mapped, how well, how many splices, how many were discarded.</p>
</div>
<div class="card">
<h4>The evidence</h4>
<p>The BAM itself — <code>flagstat</code>, <code>idxstats</code>, MAPQ, insert size, coverage. What actually landed.</p>
</div>
</div>

**Five questions:**

1. How many reads made it?
2. Where did they go?
3. How well did they align?
4. Are the pairs sane?
5. Is the coverage believable?

---

### `Log.final.out`, Annotated

| Field | Ours | What it tells you |
|---|---|---|
| Number of input reads | 5,000 | fragments in |
| Uniquely mapped reads % | **11.06%** | the headline number |
| % of reads mapped to multiple loci | 1.24% | repeats / ambiguity |
| % of reads unmapped: too short | small | over-trimming signal |
| Number of splices: Total | **443** | how much splicing was found |
| Mismatch rate per base | see log | wrong reference / contamination signal |

::: {.callout-important}
Read it top to bottom. **Every line is a failure mode** with a number attached.
:::

---

### The Denominator Trap

```text
5,000 input fragments
  × (11.06% unique + 1.24% multi) = 615 fragments
  × 2 mates                        = 1,230 primary records
  + 242 secondary                  = 1,472 records
```

`samtools flagstat` says: **1,472 total · 1,230 primary · 242 secondary**.

::: {.callout-important}
STAR counts **fragments** (pairs). `flagstat` counts **records** (mates). 11% of 5,000 is not 553 records — it is 553 **fragments**, which is 1,106 **mates**, plus multi-mappers.
:::

---

### `flagstat`, Annotated

| Line | Ours | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| in total | 1,472 | every record in the BAM |
| primary | 1,230 | one per fragment |
| secondary | 242 | extra loci for multi-mappers |
| duplicates | 0 | not marked; meaningless at this depth |
| properly paired | 1,230 (100%) | over **primary**, not input |
| read1 / read2 | 615 / 615 | the pair is balanced |

::: {.callout-note}
100% properly paired sounds perfect because it is measured over the reads that **made it into the BAM**. It says nothing about the 89% that did not map.
:::

---

### `idxstats` and the 3-Chromosome Reality

| Contig | Length | Mapped |
|---|---|---|
| `17` | 83,257,441 | **830** |
| `21` | 46,709,983 | **378** |
| `22` | 50,818,468 | **264** |
| `*` | — | 0 |

<div class="big center">830 + 378 + 264 = 1,472</div>

::: {.callout-important}
The arithmetic closes against `flagstat`. That is the single best end-to-end check in the notebook: if these do not match, one of your assumptions is wrong.
:::

---

### MAPQ: How Sure Are We?

```bash
samtools view sample.bam | cut -f5 | sort -n | uniq -c
```

Expect a **spike at 255** (unique) and a small tail at 0–3 (multi-mapping).

- MAPQ 255 is STAR’s “unique” label — it is not a probability.
- A large 0–3 tail means repeats or rRNA.
- MAPQ 0 can also mean “unmapped” — check FLAG bit 4.

::: {.callout-note}
MAPQ answers “how many places could this read come from?” — not “how correct is this base?”
:::

---

### Insert Size, Coverage, Bias

<div class="grid2">
<div class="card">
<h4>Insert size</h4>
<p><code>samtools stats | grep "insert size"</code>. A sharp peak is healthy. A bizarre spread means a library or pairing problem.</p>
</div>
<div class="card">
<h4>5′ / 3′ bias</h4>
<p>Coverage should be even across the gene. A slope means degraded RNA or a library-prep bias.</p>
</div>
<div class="card">
<h4>rRNA / chrM</h4>
<p>A few genes dominating the reads usually means rRNA contamination. chrM is absent from our reference, so we cannot see it here.</p>
</div>
<div class="card">
<h4>Strand bias</h4>
<p>Reads should not pile onto one strand unless the protocol is stranded. A strong skew means the wrong library chemistry.</p>
</div>
</div>

::: {.small .muted}
At 5,000 pairs these are concepts, not measurements. Qualimap and RNA-SeQC do them properly at real depth.
:::

---

### Red Flags

| Symptom | Usual cause | First check |
|---|---|---|
| Unique rate very low | wrong reference / contig naming / rRNA | `@SQ` names vs FASTA/GTF |
| Many “too many loci” | repeats, rRNA, short reads | `--outFilterMultimapNmax`, FastQC |
| Mismatch > 2–3% | wrong species/assembly, contamination | reference build |
| Many “too short” | over-trimming | trim settings, read length |
| 5′/3′ bias | degraded RNA / library | RIN, coverage plot |
| Duplicates > 50% | PCR over-amplification | only meaningful at real depth |

::: {.callout-note}
**One number is never a diagnosis.** The red flag is a pattern across logs, not a single threshold.
:::

---


### Is 11% Bad?

<div class="quote">
No. The denominator is the reference, not the sample.
</div>

- A whole-genome RNA-seq run expects **80–90%** unique.
- Here, only **5.85%** of the genome is indexed — and it is gene-dense.
- The honest statement for a methods section: *“11.1% of reads mapped uniquely to the three-chromosome reference; the remaining reads are outside the indexed contigs.”*

**Tools for real data:** Qualimap (5′/3′, duplication, coverage), MultiQC (aggregates logs), IGV (eyes on a locus).

---

### 👁️ Eyes on a Locus — Coverage

![](../_assets/igv.png){fig-align="center" width="94%"}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="48%"}
**chr21:8,210,178–8,219,821** — 9,645 bp, **74 records**.

- Coverage arrives in islands. Peak depth **13×**.
- **12 records** carry soft clips: `149M1S`, `88M62S`, `114M36S`.
:::
::: {.column width="52%"}
- **2** annotated exons in the window. **7 of 74** reads start inside one.
- The other 67 land off features — `Unassigned_NoFeatures` seen with eyes.

A log gives the average. **The locus shows what the average is hiding.**
:::
:::

---

### 👁️ A Spliced Locus — IGV

![](../_assets/igv_splice.png){fig-align="center" width="94%"}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="48%"}
**chr22:39,313,952–39,318,985** — gene **RPL3**, **14 records**, **7 junction arcs**.

- Longest intron: **2,020 bp** at 39,315,458–39,317,478.
- That junction has **4 uniquely-mapping** reads and **1 multi-mapping** read.
:::
::: {.column width="52%"}
- Motifs: **5 GT/AG**, **1 GC/AG**, **1 AT/AC**.
- Every arc here is annotated in the index. The arcs are the `N` in the CIGAR — you decoded one in Section 4.

::: {.callout-note}
**Load** BAM + `.bai` · FASTA · GTF. **Read** the arcs, not just the pileup.
:::
:::
:::

---

### 🖥️ Colab Session — QC + Counts

::: {.part}
<div class="label">Verify, then count</div>

- `samtools index` — build the `.bai`.
- `samtools flagstat`, `idxstats`, `stats | grep "insert size"`.
- MAPQ histogram.
- **Reproduce 615 → 1,230 → 1,472** in a markdown cell.
- `featureCounts` — then read the `.summary` rows, not just the matrix.

**Come back when the arithmetic closes.**
:::

---

### ✍️ Exercise A

**2% uniquely mapped. 70% “too many loci.”**

What is going on?

1. the reads are too short to align
2. the reads match many places in the genome
3. the reference is missing contigs

---

### ✅ Exercise A — Answer

**Option 2: the reads match many places in the genome.**

Repeats or rRNA: many loci match, so STAR reports “too many loci”
instead of guessing. Too-short reads are reported as “too short”, and a
missing contig gives unmapped reads, not a loci warning.

The wrong reference produces the same signature.

---

### ✍️ Exercise B

**95% mapped. 40% mismatch rate.**

What do you suspect?

1. the library is duplicated
2. soft-clipped bases are being counted as mismatches
3. the reference does not match the reads

---

### ✅ Exercise B — Answer

**Option 3: the reference does not match the reads.**

40% mismatch means the reference is not the species, or not the assembly
version, the reads came from. Duplicates do not raise the mismatch rate,
and soft-clipped bases are not counted as mismatches.

---

### ✍️ Exercise C

**Properly paired: 60%. Insert sizes huge.**

What is broken?

1. the library: fragments are long, pairing is off
2. the aligner is missing introns
3. `MAPQ` is too low

---

### ✅ Exercise C — Answer

**Option 1: the library.**

Long fragments and lost proper pairs are library prep and pairing. Look
at the insert size distribution before you blame the aligner: missing
introns show up in `CIGAR`, not in `FLAG`.

---

### ✍️ Exercise D

**10% of all reads land on one small contig.**

Most likely?

1. that contig is the largest in the genome
2. those reads are properly paired
3. contamination, or a contig the aligner cannot resolve

---

### ✅ Exercise D — Answer

**Option 3: contamination, or a contig the aligner cannot resolve.**

A small contig carrying 10% of the reads is rRNA, adapter, or spike-in.
It can also be a collapsed repeat: every copy maps to one place. Size and
pairing do not explain a pile-up on a small contig.

---

## 🧮 6. From BAM to Counts

::: {.agenda data-section="6"}
:::

---

### What featureCounts Takes

```bash
featureCounts -p --countReadPairs -T 2 \
  -t exon -g gene_id -a annotation.gtf \
  -o counts.txt sample.bam
```

- the BAM is the input, the GTF is the question
- `-t exon` is what to count, `-g gene_id` is what to report
- `-p --countReadPairs` counts the pair, not the two reads

---

### Fragments, Not Reads

- our BAM: 1,472 records, 1,230 primary alignments
- featureCounts read it as **736 fragments**
- **448 assigned (60.9%)** — that is the only number that becomes a count
  in the matrix

---

### The Overlap Decision

```text
BAM ──► fragment ──► overlaps an exon? ──► gene_id
                         │
                         ├── no   → Unassigned_NoFeatures
                         ├── many → Unassigned_Ambiguity
                         └── multi → Unassigned_MultiMapping
```

::: {.callout-important}
featureCounts’ own defaults, printed in its setting block: *Multimapping
reads: not counted*, *Multi-overlapping reads: not counted*, *Min
overlapping bases : 1*. A fragment that touches two genes is not split
between them.
:::

---

### Where the 736 Fragments Go

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="70%"}

![featureCounts assignment summary, measured from our run](../_assets/fc_summary.png){fig-align="center" width="100%"}

:::

::: {.column width="30%"}

- 448 assigned, 288 unassigned, 736 total

- every unassigned fragment is named by cause: multi-mapping, ambiguity,
  no features

- `Unassigned_MappingQuality` is 0: STAR’s lowest `MAPQ` here is 1, and
  the default `-q 0` filters nothing

:::

::::

---

### Strandedness Is a Choice: `-s`

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="62%"}

![Same BAM, same GTF, only `-s` changed](../_assets/fc_stranded.png){fig-align="center" width="100%"}

:::

::: {.column width="38%"}

- `-s 0` unstranded · `-s 1` forward · `-s 2` reverse

- the simulated library is unstranded, so `-s 0` keeps 448 pairs

- forcing `-s 1` gives 270 and `-s 2` gives 267: 40% of the data thrown
  away

:::

::::

::: {.callout-important}
The wrong `-s` is the most common “my matrix looks wrong” bug. Check your
library, not the tutorial you copied the command from.
:::

---

### From 448 Pairs to a Matrix

- rows: 6,661 genes, straight from the GTF
- 253 rows have a non-zero count; the sample column sums to 448
- `Chr` and `Start` list one entry per exon, separated by semicolons

---

### Read the Summary, Not Just the Matrix

::: {.callout-note}
The matrix is the numerator. **The summary is the diagnosis.** 183 + 74 + 31
is not noise: it says multimapping, overlapping genes, intergenic sequence,
in that order. If `Assigned` is low, the problem is usually alignment or
annotation — not counting.
:::

---

### 🎯 The One-Sentence Version

<div class="quote">
A FASTQ record knows its letters. It does not know where it came from.
</div>

- **Alignment** gives every read a genomic address: chromosome, position, strand.
- **A BAM** stores that address, plus the shape and confidence of the match.
- **QC** is the decision that the addresses are trustworthy enough to count.

::: {.callout-important}
Today is not “run a tool.” Today is **read what the tool produces** and decide whether to believe it.
:::

## 🚀 What's Next?
### Input Data, Normalization & PCA — from count matrix to sample structure

* **Input data**: the count matrix from `featureCounts` — genes × samples
* **Normalization**: depth differs between samples; CPM, TPM, and DESeq2 size factors put them on one scale
* **PCA**: log-transform, project. Replicates cluster; a batch shows up as one axis
* **Real data**: QC plots, sample clustering, and the first batch effect you will have to explain

::: {.callout-important}
Everything downstream inherits the BAM. A mapping you did not verify
becomes a PCA you cannot interpret.
:::
